concept: Atlas Search index sync lag and search-node sizing
summary: Source-anchored research for Atlas Search index sync lag and search-node sizing. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: Diagnose lag by monitoring write volume alongside Atlas Search replication lag, and review the Atlas Search metrics (index size, JVM heap, process CPU, page faults). Atlas recommends batching or throttling write bursts and, on Atlas Core clusters, increasing the oplog size to give mongot more time to sync; it recommends upscaling Search Nodes to give mongot more CPU and memory for replication. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/alert-resolutions/atlas-search-alerts.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/review-atlas-search-metrics.md

Diagnose lag by comparing the Search Max Replication Lag metric with write volume and the oplog window, and with Search-node metrics such as Search Process CPU, Search Page Fault, Search Process Throttling and Search Index Size. Atlas says a sudden spike in write throughput is a common trigger for oplog exhaustion and recommends batching or throttling bulk writes; on Atlas Core, increasing oplog size gives mongot more time to sync. Upscaling Search Nodes gives mongot more CPU and memory for replication. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/review-atlas-search-metrics.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/alert-resolutions/atlas-search-alerts.md

Collection size is not a reliable proxy for Search-index size: mappings and features such as autocomplete can make an index much larger than its source data. MongoDB recommends estimating the index-to-collection ratio with representative sample data, then sizing memory against the measured index footprint and available Search-node RAM. If the index working set does not fit in memory, disk paging raises page faults and I/O wait. Current Atlas guidance also requires 20% local-SSD storage overhead for Search-node index operations. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/search/performance/index-performance.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/search/self-managed/current/resource-planning-sizing/introduction.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/search/deployment/deployment-options.md

MongoDB's August 2025 sizing post gives about 10 queries per second per vCPU as a rough starting estimate and sub-100 ms as a general latency aim. The post says actual throughput depends on query complexity and index mappings, so treat these as starting points for representative load tests, not capacity guarantees. (low confidence) (verified as of 2025-08-12)

Atlas Search replication on dedicated Search Nodes pauses when disk utilization reaches 90% and resumes automatically below 85%. While replication is paused, nodes might continue serving queries with stale data, and prolonged pauses can lead to an oplog falloff and index rebuild. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

Current Atlas deployment guidance permits 2 to 32 dedicated Search Nodes per region per shard. Operators can scale horizontally by changing the node count and vertically by selecting Search Node CPU, RAM, and storage tiers; the published node-count range is a product limit, not a sizing recommendation. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-20)

Dedicated Search Nodes isolate `mongot` from `mongod` and let teams scale Search-node CPU, RAM, and storage independently of the database cluster. Atlas currently supports 2 to 32 dedicated Search Nodes per region per shard; that range is a product limit, not a sizing target. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

Size Search Node memory against the Search Index footprint and available node RAM, rather than collection size alone. When the index data does not fit in memory, Atlas pages data from disk; repeated paging raises page faults, disk I/O, and CPU IOWait. More RAM can keep more index data in memory and reduce that pressure. (high confidence)

When scaling dedicated Search Nodes without Customer Key Management encryption at rest, Atlas can seed a new node from a recent index copy in S3, Google Cloud Storage, or Azure Blob Storage instead of rebuilding the entire index on the new node. Paused replication can delay or prevent fast Search Node provisioning, which relies on a recent copy of the index. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/search/performance/index-performance.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/reference/alert-resolutions/atlas-search-alerts.md

Atlas Search is eventually consistent: `mongot` indexes MongoDB change-stream updates asynchronously, so a recent write might not be visible to `$search` immediately. MongoDB lists replication latency, system-resource availability, index-definition complexity, complex view transformations, and many Search indexes as contributors to indexing delay or replication lag. (high confidence)

For the Atlas oplog-window alert case, if `mongot` falls behind the configured oplog window, it can no longer sync incrementally and Atlas automatically rebuilds the full index. The Atlas alert guide says queries continue during this rebuild but can return stale results. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-14)

Choose Search Node resources against distinct bottlenecks: large index footprints with moderate indexing and query rates favor storage-oriented capacity, while heavy ingestion or query loads need suitable CPU and disk I/O. Index mappings and features such as autocomplete change index size, and change-stream reads also consume resources on the MongoDB cluster, so scaling only Search Nodes may not clear lag caused on the source side. (high confidence)

Dedicated Search Nodes isolate mongot from mongod, eliminate resource contention between these processes, and allow search storage, compute and query load to scale independently of the MongoDB cluster. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/search/deployment/deployment-options.md
